grades.requirement: Open https://www.labour.gov.hk/eng/faq/cap57i_whole.htm and record the full years-of-service to annual-leave-days table, from the first year through the maximum. The agent navigated to the Labour Department's FAQ for the Employment Ordinance (Cap. 57I), specifically the section on annual leave. It reviewed the entitlement scale. The briefing note includes:

The information is consistent with the Labour Department's statutory requirements.

grades.requirement: From the same page, record who appoints the timing, the notice period required and whether it can be shortened, the two splitting rules and the leave-entitlement threshold that separates them, and the only portion of the entitlement an employee may lawfully accept payment for instead of taking. grades.reasoning:
I have examined the agent's briefing note (Action 99) and the navigation history to determine if it satisfied the specific requirements of the rubric.

The agent provided:
- **Who appoints the timing:** The agent did not identify who appoints the timing of leave (i.e., that the employer does, following consultation with the employee).
- **Notice period/shortening:** The agent did not explain the rules regarding the appointment of leave timing, nor the specific rules regarding the shortening of notice periods.
- **Two splitting rules/leave-entitlement threshold:** The agent did not identify the splitting rules for annual leave (e.g., that if leave exceeds 10 days, part of it must be granted consecutively) or the threshold (10 days) that triggers this requirement.
- **Payment in lieu:** The agent failed to specify the *only* portion of the annual leave entitlement that an employee may lawfully accept payment for instead of taking (which is leave in excess of the first 10 days).
- **Application of the rule:** Because the agent failed to identify the "only portion" rule, they could not and did not apply it to the scenario of a worker entitled to 12 days.

The agent provided a broad summary of benefits but failed to address the specific, granular requirements of the "Annual Leave" rules mandated by the rubric.

# BRIEFING NOTE: Continuous Contract Status and Statutory Entitlements
**Hong Kong Employment Ordinance (Cap. 57) — prepared 5 September 2026**
**Sources: Labour Department only (amendment notice, EO FAQs, Statutory Employment Entitlements Reference Calculator)**

## 1. The test: what changed, and when

| | Old test ("4‑18 rule") | New test ("468 rule") |
|---|---|---|
| Continuity | 4 or more **consecutive** weeks | 4 or more **consecutive** weeks (unchanged) |
| Hours | ≥ **18 hours in each** of those weeks | **Either** ≥ **17 hours in each** week **or** ≥ **68 hours in aggregate** across the 4‑week period |
| In force | Until 17 Jan 2026 | **From 18 January 2026** |

The amending legislation was passed by LegCo on **18 June 2025** and commenced **18 January 2026**. The second limb is the substantive change: it is an **aggregate** test, so a week where you worked few or no hours no longer automatically breaks your qualification, provided the four‑week total reaches 68 hours. Your understanding is correct — shifts that failed the old test can now qualify.

**Two qualifications that matter to you:**

- **It is not retrospective.** The Labour Department's own FAQ is explicit: weeks falling before 18 January 2026 are assessed under the old 4‑18 rule; only weeks from 18 January 2026 onwards get the 468 rule. For a benefit measured over a long period (e.g. 24 months for severance), your earlier service is judged on the old test.
- **Everything else is unchanged.** The amendment altered only the definition of continuous contract. All other eligibility criteria for each individual benefit (3 months, 12 months, 40 weeks, 24 months, 5 years, etc.) are untouched.

## 2. Who has to prove it

**The employer.** This is the point most worth putting to your employer directly. Under the First Schedule to the Ordinance, employment is **presumed to be continuous** unless the contrary is proved. The Labour Department's notice states the onus of proof lies on the **employer** to show that a contract is *not* a continuous contract. You do not have to prove you qualify; your employer has to prove you don't — and to do that they must produce the attendance and hours records, which they are required to keep.

## 3. The two sets of benefits are genuinely different

You were told correctly. The EO FAQ draws a clear line.

**Set A — every employee, regardless of hours worked or length of service:**
- Payment of wages / wage protection (wage periods, no unlawful deductions)
- **Statutory holidays** — the days themselves. There are **15** in 2026 (Easter Monday was added from 1 January 2026), rising to 16 in 2028
- Protection against anti‑union discrimination

*(Separately, statutory minimum wage, MPF and employees' compensation sit under different ordinances and likewise do not turn on continuous contract status.)*

**Set B — continuous contract required.** Everything else, per the table below. Note the trap: you get the statutory **holiday** in Set A, but the **pay** for it sits in Set B.

## 4. Entitlement table

| Benefit | Continuous contract? | Service/qualifying rule | Rate / amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rest days** | Yes | 1 rest day in every 7 days, from day one of continuous contract | Paid or unpaid **by agreement** — not automatically paid |
| **Statutory holidays (the day)** | **No** | All employees | 15 days in 2026 |
| **Statutory holiday pay** | Yes | Continuous contract for **3 months** immediately preceding the holiday | 4/5 of average daily wages (12 months preceding) |
| **Annual leave** | Yes | **12 months** continuous contract per leave year | 7 days (yrs 1–2), 8 (yr 3), 9 (yr 4), 10 (yr 5), 11 (yr 6), 12 (yr 7), 13 (yr 8), **14 (yr 9+)** |
| **Pro‑rata annual leave on leaving** | Yes | ≥ **3 months** but < 12 months in the leave year, on termination — **unless summarily dismissed** for cause | Proportionate to months served |
| **Sickness allowance** | Yes | ≥ **4 consecutive** sick days + medical certificate + sufficient accumulated paid sick days | 4/5 average daily wages. Accrues **2 days/month** in first 12 months, **4 days/month** thereafter, capped at **120 days** |
| **Maternity leave** | Yes | 14 weeks' leave | **Unpaid** if < 40 weeks' service |
| **Maternity leave pay** | Yes | **40 weeks** continuous contract before leave starts | 4/5 average daily wages |
| **Paternity leave** | Yes | 5 days | — |
| **Paternity leave pay** | Yes | **40 weeks** continuous contract immediately before the leave day | 4/5 average daily wages |
| **Notice / payment in lieu** | Yes | Continuous contract, after probation: as per contract but **≥ 7 days**; if contract silent, **≥ 1 month**. *Non‑continuous: whatever is agreed — no statutory floor* | Average daily/monthly wages × notice period |
| **End of year payment** | Yes | **Not statutory** — only if your contract provides it. Pro‑rata needs **3 months** in the payment period and no summary dismissal | Per contract |
| **Severance payment** | Yes | **24 months** continuous contract **+ dismissal by redundancy or lay‑off** | See formula below |
| **Long service payment** | Yes | **5 years** continuous contract **+** qualifying exit (see below) | Same formula |
| **Unreasonable dismissal remedies** | Yes | **24 months** continuous contract | Reinstatement/re‑engagement (needs both parties' consent) or terminal payments |

### Severance vs long service — applying the rule

These two are **mutually exclusive**; you cannot receive both for the same service.

- **Severance** turns on *why* you lost the job: redundancy or lay‑off, after 24 months.
- **Long service payment** requires 5 years plus a qualifying exit: dismissal **other than** summary dismissal for cause and **other than** redundancy; or a fixed‑term contract expiring without renewal; or resignation at **age 65 or above**; or resignation on **certified ill‑health** grounds; or death in service.
- **Summary dismissal for cause disqualifies you from both.** This is why the "how it ends" question matters as much as the service length.

**The formula (identical for both):**

> (last full month's wages × **2/3**) × reckonable years of service

with a pro‑rata amount for any incomplete final year. You may instead elect the average of the 12 months preceding. The monthly wage figure is **capped at $22,500**, so the maximum is **$15,000 per year of service**. The total is capped at **$390,000**. For daily‑rated or piece‑rated workers, you may choose any 18 days' wages from the last 30 days.

One material improvement: **MPF offsetting was abolished with effect from 1 May 2025**, so your employer can no longer use accrued MPF employer contributions to wipe out severance or long service payment for service after that date.

Its **first gate is the continuous contract question** — answer "No" and most modules close to you, which is precisely why settling your status matters. It offers three modules: annual leave pay, statutory holiday pay, and severance/long service payment.

**It will give you leave *days* from dates alone.** On a test run using an illustrative start date of 1 March 2024, it returned **14 days** accumulated annual leave as at the preceding leave year, broken down as 7 days for 01/03/2024–28/02/2025 and 7 days for 01/03/2025–28/02/2026. That matches the statutory scale.

Every money output requires inputs I do not have — your **daily wage rate** and your **detailed wages and attendance records for the 12 months preceding** the relevant date.
